verdicts.summary: The only hazard I could find in the single mapSettingsSecrets walk is the hand-kept providerSecretFields map, which finding 0 already reports. Secret names for env, host and usage-limit match the old helpers.
The load-time move only redacts secrets whose store write succeeded. A failed write leaves the plaintext in the file and it is retried on the next load. The missing log context is finding 1.
verdicts.scenario: secretStore.set fails for one of two pending field secrets (say the Antigravity apiKey OK, the GitHub token fails). Only the secret that was stored is turned into the marker. The file is rewritten with the token still in plaintext, so it keeps working and is retried on the next load. I also tried writeSettingsAtomically failing after set succeeds: the file still holds the plaintext and the next load sets the same value again.

verdicts.summary: Every ws.ts path that sends settings to the client (get, update response, stream) goes through redactServerSettingsForClient. When the client sends the marker back, the stored value is kept.
verdicts.scenario: The client gets the marker for the Antigravity apiKey and upserts the instance unchanged. persistSettingsSecrets sees secret.redacted, and the old cached entry is also redacted, so inlineValue is undefined. The value is kept: no write, and no stale removal because the name goes into nextSecretNames. When the earlier move failed and the cache still held plaintext, inlineValue is that plaintext and it gets written to the store.

verdicts.summary: The marker showing up in the card/dialog variants is finding 2. The new inability to clear a provider-config secret is reported separately below as an added hazard.
The settingsSecret flag survives withDecodingDefault and a later annotateKey, whichever order is used. The bitbucket inline settingsSecret also works.
verdicts.scenario: Antigravity apiKey: secretSetting, then withDecodingDefault, then annotateKey(title...). withDecodingDefault builds its result through decodeTo(self), and appendTransformation keeps `to`'s AST via replaceEncoding, so the context still carries settingsSecret. The later annotateKey merges into the existing annotations. Bitbucket passes settingsSecret inside the annotateKey after withDecodingDefault. The server test asserts that the Antigravity apiKey is redacted.

verdicts.summary: No reference to the removed helper remains outside vendored code. Host secret fields now come from secretSettingsFields for each definition.
verdicts.scenario: I searched the repo (excluding node_modules and .repos) for secretSourceControlHostSettingsFields and for providerSettingsForm.secret readers. There are no hits other than doc comments. Bitbucket, GitHub and GitCafe all still declare their secret fields.

verdicts.summary: A saved Antigravity apiKey can no longer be cleared from the provider settings UI.
verdicts.scenario: 1) A user has saved an Antigravity apiKey. 2) In ProviderInstanceCard (variant="settings", ProviderInstanceCard.tsx:1150-1156) the field is now a SecretInput with value="" and configured=true. 3) The user wants to remove the key, for example to switch to Vertex or OAuth. Leaving the input empty never commits: useCommitOnBlur skips when the draft equals "", and SecretInput.tsx:32 drops an empty commit when configured. 4) ProviderSettingsForm offers no clear button for config secrets. The env-var rows do have one (ProviderInstanceCard.tsx:297-307). Before this change apiKey was a plain DraftInput showing the saved value, so deleting the text and blurring committed "" and the server removed it.
verdicts.consequence: The key stays in the secret store and keeps being used. The only ways to remove it are deleting the instance or hand-editing settings.json.

verdicts.summary: If reading the secret store fails during a settings change, providers receive the literal marker as the Antigravity apiKey.
verdicts.scenario: 1) A settings update is persisted, and emitChange(next) publishes settings in which field secrets hold "••••••" (settingsSecrets.ts:74). 2) In materializeChanges, secretStore.get fails, for example because the keychain is locked or unreadable. 3) The catch logs a warning and emits the unmaterialized settings. 4) ProviderHostLive / ProviderInstanceRegistryHydration subscribe to these changes, so the Antigravity driver gets apiKey "••••••" and sends it to Gemini. Env secrets in the same path get value "". Host and usage-limit fields behaved this way before; the apiKey is newly exposed to it.
verdicts.consequence: Antigravity requests fail authentication with a bogus key instead of failing clearly. Only a generic warning is logged.
